sections.title: The Intuitive Shift: Discrete vs. Continuous
sections.content: Briefly review discrete probability mass functions (histograms). Introduce the limitation of 'pinpoint' probabilities in continuous spaces: the probability of a specific exact value (like exactly 1.7000...m height) is zero. Transition to the concept of 'density'—the likelihood of falling within an interval.
sections.example: Comparing a dice roll (discrete points) to measuring the exact time a digital stopwatch stops (continuous interval).

sections.title: Visualizing the Curve
sections.content: Define the PDF as a non-negative function f(x) where the total area under the curve equals 1. Use an animation showing a histogram with shrinking bin widths that eventually smooths into a continuous curve.
sections.example: A 'Robot Battery Life' chart: The curve is higher where the robot is most likely to die, lower at the extremes.

sections.title: Defining Probability as Area
sections.content: Explain that P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the definite integral of f(x) from a to b. Visually represent this as shading the area under the curve between two points.
sections.example: Calculating the probability that a 'Delivery Drone' arrives between 10:00 AM and 10:15 AM by calculating the area of that specific slice on the time-distribution curve.

sections.title: Properties and Constraints
sections.content: Summarize the two golden rules for a valid PDF: 1) f(x) ≥ 0 for all x; 2) The integral over the entire domain equals 1. Use a visual 'Normalization' effect where a graph is scaled to ensure the total area is exactly one unit.
sections.example: A 'Cat Jump Height' graph that must be perfectly shaped so that the total probability of all possible jump heights sums to 100%.

sections.title: Conclusion and Application
sections.content: Recap: PDF is not probability itself, but the 'density' of probability. Reiterate that we find probability by finding area. Final visual summary connecting the graph to real-world risk management.
sections.example: Predicting the survival time of a simulated creature in a game environment using a standard normal distribution PDF.
